introduction: After Shrewsbury, England remains unsettled: a fresh rebellion gathers while King Henry IV grows ill and worries about his heir. Prince Hal moves between obligations at court and the tavern world of Falstaff, whose wit keeps creditors, officers and age itself at bay. As soldiers assemble and royal authority passes towards a new generation, promises of loyalty, reform and reward become difficult to trust. The approaching succession tests both political alliances and the claims of old friendship.

fullSynopsis.text: Rumour announces that its flattering reports of rebel victory at Shrewsbury are false. Northumberland initially welcomes such news, but an eyewitness confirms Hotspur's death and the King's victory. Grief turns him towards revenge, and the Archbishop of York's renewed rising offers an ally. The Archbishop and his fellow rebels debate their resources, warning against repeating Hotspur's fatal reliance on uncertain reinforcements. Northumberland nevertheless withdraws to Scotland after Lady Percy bitterly recalls his failure to support her husband. The remaining leaders must face the royal army without him.

Falstaff, meanwhile, meets age, illness and poverty with unflagging verbal ingenuity. The Lord Chief Justice rebukes his conduct and refuses to lend him money. Mistress Quickly tries to arrest him for debt and says that he promised to marry her, but he persuades her to withdraw her action and offer another loan. Hal tells Poins that his father's illness genuinely grieves him, though his dissolute reputation would make public tears seem hypocritical. The two disguise themselves as tavern drawers and overhear Falstaff disparaging them while he courts Doll Tearsheet. Exposed, he invents another defence, until urgent military business ends the entertainment.

The sleepless King reflects on the burdens of rule and the instability of the alliances that raised him. Warwick reassures him about the rebellion and reports Glendower dead, but Henry's sickness and anxiety persist. In Gloucestershire, Falstaff recruits soldiers with the help of Justices Shallow and Silence. Shallow boasts of their youthful exploits; privately Falstaff calls his recollections lies and sees his property as an opportunity for profit. Bardolph accepts money from Mouldy and Bullcalf to obtain their release, and Falstaff dismisses them while selecting less imposing alternatives, including Feeble, whose willingness to serve contrasts with the corruption around him.

At Gaultree Forest, Westmoreland negotiates with the Archbishop, Mowbray and Hastings. Prince John promises to redress their grievances and proposes that both armies disperse. Once the rebels' soldiers have gone, however, the royal troops remain, and the rebel leaders are arrested for treason. John denies having promised them immunity and orders them to execution. Arriving late, Falstaff acquires Colevile's surrender largely through the fame of his name and demands recognition for his supposed prowess. John sends the prisoner to execution too; Falstaff turns back towards Shallow's hospitality.

News of these successes and of Northumberland's separate defeat reaches Henry, but relief brings another collapse. Left watching his apparently lifeless father, Hal takes the crown and asserts his inheritance. Henry wakes, discovers it missing, and accuses his son of wishing him dead. Hal returns it, explains his mistake and professes grief rather than ambition. Reconciled, Henry acknowledges the crooked means by which he gained the throne and advises foreign wars to divert dangerous minds from domestic grievances. Learning that the room of his collapse is called Jerusalem, he asks to be carried there, interpreting a prophecy he had understood geographically.

Henry's death brings Hal to the throne as Henry V. The Chief Justice fears vengeance because he once imprisoned the Prince for striking him in court. Instead, the new King approves his defence of royal justice, confirms his office and asks for his guidance. At Shallow's house, Pistol's news of the succession sends Falstaff rushing to London, confident that he can distribute offices and override the law. Quickly and Doll, meanwhile, are dragged away by officers over an alleged fatal assault; Quickly still hopes for Falstaff's protection.

Following the coronation, Falstaff greets his old companion familiarly, only to meet a public rejection. Henry forbids him and his former associates to approach within ten miles of his person on pain of death, while promising maintenance and the possibility of advancement if they reform. Falstaff insists that favour will return in private, despite Shallow's worried request for repayment of his thousand pounds. The Chief Justice sends Falstaff and his company to the Fleet prison. John welcomes the new order and anticipates a campaign in France. The epilogue asks indulgence and promises a continuation, speculating about Falstaff's future rather than staging his death.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Rumour's false tale of royal defeat reaches Northumberland through Lord Bardolph, but Travers brings contrary tidings and Morton confirms that Hotspur is dead. Northumberland throws off his sickroom restraints in a surge of grief and fury. His supporters urge deliberation, and news that the Archbishop of York is raising an army directs his thoughts towards renewed resistance. In London, Falstaff answers the Chief Justice's rebukes with jokes, evasions and claims to youth. His supposed military distinction has helped obscure the Gadshill robbery, but he remains short of money and bound for service under Prince John. At York, the rebel leaders debate whether their present strength can sustain the venture without Northumberland. Lord Bardolph warns against relying on imagined supplies, while Hastings argues that the King's divided commitments give them a chance.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: Quickly employs officers to arrest Falstaff for debt, accusing him of exploiting both her purse and his promise to marry her. The Chief Justice supports her complaint, yet Falstaff cajoles her into withdrawing it and offering him more money. Hal admits to Poins that he is worried about his sick father, but believes his reputation prevents a credible display of sorrow. They arrange to visit Falstaff disguised as drawers. Elsewhere, Lady Percy reproaches Northumberland for leaving Hotspur unsupported, and he resolves to withdraw to Scotland. In the tavern, Falstaff drives out the swaggering Pistol and settles into affectionate banter with Doll. Hal and Poins overhear him belittling them; caught, he claims he was protecting them from wicked admirers. News from Westminster and the northern army finally calls the men away.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: Unable to sleep, Henry envies the rest available to his poorest subjects and reflects on the burdens of sovereignty. He recalls Richard's prediction that Northumberland would turn against the king he had helped advance, wondering whether these betrayals are inevitable. Warwick interprets the apparent prophecy through human character, discounts exaggerated reports of rebel strength and brings news that Glendower is dead. Henry still hopes to undertake his long-delayed journey to the Holy Land. In Gloucestershire, Shallow and Silence receive Falstaff and help muster recruits. Shallow's nostalgic boasting prompts Falstaff's private contempt, but his wealth invites exploitation. Mouldy and Bullcalf pay Bardolph to secure exemption; Falstaff releases them and praises less imposing substitutes. Feeble accepts the possibility of death with plain courage, while Falstaff leaves intending to profit from Shallow on his return.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: The northern rebels learn that Northumberland has withdrawn. Westmoreland offers negotiations, and John accepts their demands for redress, inviting both armies to disperse. When the rebels disband, their leaders are arrested; John insists he promised remedies, not pardon, and sends them to death. Falstaff arrives late, takes Colevile's voluntary surrender and seeks credit before returning towards Gloucestershire. At Westminster, reports of victory and Northumberland's defeat precede Henry's collapse. Hal, thinking him dead, takes the crown; the waking King reads this as eager anticipation of his death. Hal returns it and pleads his grief, winning reconciliation. Henry admits the troubled origins of his kingship and recommends foreign quarrels to distract restless subjects. Told that his earlier chamber is named Jerusalem, he asks to return there to die, finding an unexpected meaning in an old prophecy.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: Falstaff enjoys Shallow's hospitality and plans to turn the household's peculiarities into entertainment for Hal. After Henry IV's death, the Chief Justice expects punishment for having imprisoned the Prince, but Henry V commends his impartiality and retains him as an adviser. Pistol brings Falstaff the news of accession; he promises honours to his friends and rides to London, imagining unlimited influence. Quickly and Doll are taken into custody over an alleged killing. Falstaff's greeting after the coronation meets Henry's public repudiation: the former companions must keep ten miles away, though they will receive support and may gain advancement through reform. Falstaff calls the rejection a performance, but Shallow fears for his loan. The Chief Justice sends the company to the Fleet, while John predicts war in France under the reformed King.

framing.label: INDUCTION
framing.summary: Rumour appears covered in tongues and explains how conjecture and false reports travel. It acknowledges the King's victory at Shrewsbury, then describes spreading the opposite story: Hotspur has supposedly killed Hal and Douglas has killed Henry. These comforting lies are already reaching Northumberland, preparing the audience to distinguish hopeful hearsay from the truth of the opening scene.

framing.label: EPILOGUE
framing.summary: A performer asks the audience to forgive the play's shortcomings, compares the audience's forgiveness to relief from debt, and offers dancing as another form of repayment. The speaker promises a continuation involving Katharine of France and Sir John, and speculates that Falstaff may die of a sweat. This remains a theatrical promise, not an event in the play. The speech also distinguishes Falstaff from the martyred Oldcastle.
